name: Louisiana

notes: Food for home (what SNAP can buy, candy and soft drinks included) is exempt from the 5% state tax; parish and city taxes apply to it at their full rate, except where the local rate listing gives a lower rate on food (in New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Lafayette, Monroe and some other cities and parishes), which is used there.
Alcohol is taxed at the full rate, on top of excise taxes left out here (liquor 80 cents a liter, beer $12.50 a barrel).

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the full rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: $1.08 a pack of cigarettes, 15 cents a milliliter of vapor liquid, 20% of the invoice price on smokeless tobacco and 33% on smoking tobacco.
Personal care products: diapers and feminine hygiene products are exempt from state and local sales taxes (R.S. 47:305.75, as amended in 2025), which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed.
Laundry and dry cleaning: laundering and dry cleaning are taxed; coin-operated self-service laundry isn't.
Motor fuel is exempt from state and local sales taxes and pays a 20-cent-a-gallon excise tax instead, left out here.
Repair services to tangible personal property are taxable.
The state rate is 5% from January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2029, then 4.75% (Act 11 of the 2024 Third Extraordinary Session).
Louisiana's sales tax holidays were repealed, except the Second Amendment holiday on firearms, ammunition and hunting supplies (September 4 to 6, 2026), which is not taken out here.

Hotel stays pay sales tax plus local occupancy taxes (in New Orleans, the Exhibition Hall Authority, tourism and other occupancy taxes and fees bring the total to about 15% to 17%), which are not counted here.
Louisiana did not answer the 2017 FTA survey; the services below are from state law.
gaps: The Commission's listing is effective July 1, 2025, the latest posted when downloaded in October 2026, so later changes appear only where an official source confirms them. East Baton Rouge's own July 1, 2026 rate chart confirms new districts there (the Southern University and LSU economic development districts, the LSU Athletic Subdistrict and Bayou Fountain). Applied from the parish collectors' own rate tables: Opelousas' city tax to 2.2% (October 1, 2025), Washington's (St. Landry Parish) to 1.2% (January 1, 2026) and West Feliciana Parish's rate outside St. Francisville down 0.5% when its recreation tax ended (October 1, 2026); Breaux Bridge's Northern Annex to 2% (October 1, 2025) is noted on its page. Other changes reported by US Geocoder (from the Louisiana Association of Tax Administrators) but not yet confirmed by the collectors: the Northshore Square district's tax rescinded (January 1, 2026); Oakdale's city rate to 1.3% and the Jefferson Davis Parish School Board's to 2.5% (April 1, 2026); Sterlington's district rate down 1% (July 1, 2026).

Economic development, school, fire, road, hospital and annexation districts that cover part of a city or parish are not applied; where higher, they set the top of its range, and the city's or parish's page names them.

2 entries for the part of a city in a neighboring parish are covered by that city's own entry; Arnaudville, Bossier City, Broussard, DeRidder, Delcambre, Duson, Eunice, Junction City and Shreveport have a part in a second parish with its own rate, and a tract at least half in such a city takes the rate of its own parish part.

Food for home is exempt from the state tax; local taxes apply to it at the full local rate except where the listing gives a lower rate on food: in all of East Baton Rouge, Jefferson, Lafayette, Plaquemines, St. John the Baptist and West Baton Rouge parishes, in Calcasieu and Washington parishes outside their cities, in New Orleans (Orleans Parish), and in the cities of Angie, Franklinton, Monroe and Varnado.
Not matched to a Census place, so those areas take the parish rate: St. George (incorporated in 2024, not yet a Census place; its rate equals the parish's)

programs: Economic development districts are mapped for East Baton Rouge Parish (Baton Rouge, Baker and St. George), Shreveport and Lafayette Parish (Lafayette, Scott, Carencro and Broussard, from Lafayette Consolidated Government's layer), along with New Orleans' TIF districts and Baton Rouge's sales-tax TIF districts and Downtown Development District. New Orleans' economic development districts (among them the French Quarter's) and its Downtown Development District aren't mapped: the city's layer gives their names but not their boundaries. Lake Charles' map service draws a North Lake Charles redevelopment district and its downtown development district's area, but what each levies or captures wasn't confirmed, so they aren't drawn here (the City's service is offered as is, for information only). The Enterprise Zone block groups are those that qualified in 2023; the program took no new projects after June 30, 2025 (Louisiana Economic Development).

warn.text: New Orleans draws many visitors, but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (4.3%) and its 458 lodging places (1.2 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 27 of its 184 tracts, among them the French Quarter's and the Central Business District's, are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Natchitoches draws many visitors (its historic district and its Christmas Festival), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (1.3%) and its 27 lodging places (1.8 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, though one of its 4 census tracts is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Breaux Bridge draws many visitors (its crawfish festival and nearby Lake Martin), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (4.3%) and its 5 lodging places (0.6 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Brownsville may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its hotels and motels along Interstate 20 (14 lodging places, 5.1 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.
Carlyss' flag as a visitor economy rests on its 16 lodging places (2.5 per 1,000 residents), which likely serve work travel to the area's plants more than tourists, so read that flag with care.

New Llano's flag as a visitor economy rests on its 5 lodging places (2.2 per 1,000 residents), next to Fort Johnson, an Army post; they likely serve people traveling to the post more than tourists, so read that flag with care.
